rows: Two 1/4" x 2" or longer lag screws

steps: Uncrate
Remove the crate top, supports and plastic cover; remove the pallet lag bolts with a 7/16"(12mm) wrench.
Fit the side panels
Pattern at the top, slide the front tabs into the Panel Mounting Bracket slots and pull back to engage; fasten with the supplied screws (fibre washers on enamel panels).
Floor protector
Continuous non-combustible ember protection on a combustible floor: USA 16" (406 mm) front and 8" (203 mm) sides of the loading door opening, also under the connector plus 2" (51 mm) each side.
Position & clearances
Set floor protector and stove to the rating-label clearances; use a listed double-wall connector for close clearances.

Clearance values are on the rating label (see the Clearances spec). Clearances may be reduced with heat shielding/insulating materials: consult CSA B365 or NFPA 211 and local fire codes and authorities for approval. For close clearances, use a listed double-wall connector.

  • Freestanding only: not in any fireplace, never connected to an air distribution duct.
  • Pedestal or leg kit must be attached; don't obstruct the space beneath the heater.
  • Never installed in a makeshift or "temporary" manner.

Fig. 6 shows the residential clearance layouts as a drawing.
Chimney & connector check

6" flue to a dedicated UL-103HT / ULC-S629 listed or lined masonry chimney, 15 feet (4.6 m.) minimum system height; exit 3 feet (1 m.) above the roof and two feet (0.6 m.) above anything within 10 feet (3 m.).
Run the chimney & connector
Plumb-bob from the flue center to mark ceiling and roof, clear joists and rafters, install the listed chimney to the rain cap, then the connector: crimped end into the collar, three screws.

1. Position the floor protection and stove per the clearances.
  2. Mark the ceiling and roof hole with a string and plumb-bob over the exact center of the flue.
  3. Check for floor joists, ceiling joists and rafters; adjust and reconfirm clearances.
  4. Install the listed chimney from the ceiling through to the rain cap per its manufacturer (may include framing in holes).
  5. Slip the connector's crimped edge inside the stove collar; secure with three screws through the collar holes.
  6. Add the remaining lengths up to the chimney and secure with the manufacturer's approved adapter; a slip section makes this easier.

Single-wall connector

  • As short and straight as possible: six inch diameter, 24 gauge black pipe, clean and in new condition.
  • Crimped (male) ends pointing down; 3 sheet metal screws at every joint and collar.
  • Never through an attic, roof space, closet or similar concealed space, floor or ceiling; through a combustible wall only per CAN/CSA-B365 or NFPA 211.

Offsets: at least three sheet metal screws per joint on all connector, offset elbow and chimney sections, supported by the chimney manufacturer's listed offset support. Up-and-out installs: 12" [305mm] minimum first section of pipe; give it as much vertical length as possible or the unit may be harder to start.
Combustion air

Outside air (required in mobile homes, optional residential): 4" Intake Starter on the Ash Box Enclosure, 4"(100mm) i.d. metal flex through the floor or the wall behind; secure the stove to the structure.
Through-wall pass (if used)
Pass a combustible wall only with NFPA 211 System A, B, C or D (12, 9, 6 or 2 in. minimum to combustibles); keep the vapour barrier intact.

As per NFPA 211-2013. The vapour barrier must be maintained wherever the chimney or other components penetrate to the exterior.

System A · 12 in. (305mm)Min. 3.5 in. (90 mm) brick wall; 12 in. (305 mm) brick from clay liner to combustibles; fireclay liner min. 5/8 in. (16 mm) wall
System B · 9 in. (229mm)Solid-insulated listed chimney length, 1 in. (25.4 mm) or more insulation, 9 in. (229 mm) air space to combustibles
System C · 6 in. (152mm)24 gauge connector and ventilated thimble with two 1 in. (25.4 mm) air channels, 6 in. (152 mm) glass fiber insulation
System D · 2 in. (51mm)Solid-insulated listed chimney length 2 in. (51 mm) larger than the connector, min. 12 in. (305 mm) long, 2 in. (51 mm) air space

Supports fastened to wall surfaces on all sides; fasteners must not penetrate the chimney liner.
Mobile home
Listed double-wall connector, outside air, two 1/4" x 2" or longer lag screws to the floor; not in a sleeping room, no horizontal connector.
Firebrick & blower
Confirm the brick layout (rear wall, side walls, floor; one spare "A" brick). Blower kit 11140001 can be added any time; route its cord away from the stove.

Brick A9" X 4 1/2" X 1 1/4" (230 mm x 115 mm x 32 mm)
Brick B2" X 9" X 1 1/4" (57 mm x 230 mm x 32 mm)
Brick C4 1/2" X 4 1/2" X 1 1/4" (115 mm x 115 mm x 32 mm)
Brick D2" X 4 1/2" X 1 1/4" (57mm x 115 mm x 32 mm)

Start with the rear wall, then each side wall, then the floor; the placement is shown brick by brick in Figs. 14 to 22. One full-size "A" brick is left over as a spare. Firebrick set: part 80000248.

Blower kit (Part #: 11140001): three-prong cord; follow the kit's instructions; route the power cord away from the heater, never beneath it.

Fire too small → build a larger fire; open the draft control to raise the burn rate
Draft too low → chimney plugged or restricted; inspect and clean

items: Air control set too high → set it lower
Not enough wood → unsplit wood is preferred

Chimney plugged or restricted → inspect and clean

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Build every fire directly on the firebricks. Don't use a grate or andirons to raise the wood.

  1. Move the air control to High (all the way to the left) and open the door.
  2. Put crumpled newspaper in the centre of the stove and crisscross several pieces of dry kindling over it. Add a few small pieces of dry wood on top.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door open a crack, about 1/2" (13mm) to 1" (25mm), until the kindling is fully in flames.
  4. Add a few small logs and close the door.
  5. Once there's a good bed of coals and the wood has charred, set the air control for normal burning.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or any similar liquid to start or "freshen up" a fire. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine.

Your first few fires

The paint bakes on during the first 2-3 fires. Open all windows and doors so the room is well ventilated, because the smoke and fumes can bother some people. Follow the Stove Bright (Forrest Paint) sheet that came with your stove. Smoke detectors may go off more often while the paint cures. Don't disconnect them.

air.title: Burning, reloading & overnight fires
air.html:
Once the fire is going, set the air control where you want it. Every home is different, so the right setting takes some trial and error. Note what works for next time.

  • Smoke rolling down the glass (a "waterfall") means you turned the air down too soon or too low.
  • High ("H") is the maximum firing rate. Use it only to start a fire or preheat a fresh load.
  • Keep the door closed while burning. This stove isn't designed to burn with the door open.
  • The lowest burn setting is fixed at the factory and must not be altered.

Adding wood

  1. Turn the air control to high and give the fire time to brighten.
  2. Open the door slowly. This keeps smoke from puffing back out.
  3. Load wood endwise, mixing shapes and sizes up to 18" (457mm) long, so air can flow between the logs. Don't stack it so high that opening the door would be hazardous.

Overnight burns

Unsplit logs work best. Char the load completely on the maximum setting before you turn the air down. Never try to burn overnight with green or wet wood.

In the morning, rake the hot embers to the front, add a couple of dry split logs, close the door and set the air to high. Once the wood chars, reset the air control.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn natural wood only. Air-dried, seasoned hardwood gives more heat and less smoke than softwood or green wood.

  • Season (air dry) wood for six months or more.
  • Store it under cover, away from open flame or heat sources.
  • Wet wood smoulders, makes heavy smoke and creosote, gives little heat and tends to go out. It can cut heat output by up to 25%.

Test a piece

Put a large piece on a good, large bed of coals:

  • Dry: it burns on more than one side within one minute.
  • Damp: it turns black and lights within three minutes.
  • Too wet: it sizzles, hisses and blackens without lighting in five minutes. Don't burn it.

Never burn

Salt water wood, treated wood, wet or green wood, coal or charcoal, garbage, solvents, lawn clippings or yard waste, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, anything containing rubber, plastic or asbestos, construction or demolition debris, petroleum waste, paints, paint thinners, asphalt products, paper products, cardboard, plywood or particleboard.

Charcoal and other fuels can make large amounts of carbon monoxide, a gas you can't taste or smell that can kill. Never barbecue in this stove. Salt water wood and garbage contain chlorides that quickly destroy metal and void the warranty.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Only remove ashes when the stove is cold. When ashes get 3" (76mm) to 4" (102mm) deep and the fire has burned down and cooled, take out the excess. Leave about 1" (25 mm) of ash on the firebox floor. It helps keep a hot charcoal bed.

Using the ash dump

  1. The handle is behind the Lower Grill, under the ash lip on the left. Pull the Lower Grill up to unlock it, then tip it toward you.
  2. Pull the handle out 1/2" (13mm) and turn it clockwise. This unlocks the ash dump so it can open.
  3. Hold the handle open and pull ashes into the opening. Avoid large embers; they still have heat in them.
  4. Release the handle and push it in to lock. Make sure the ash dump door is properly closed, then fill the cavity with the remaining ash, level with the firebox floor.
  5. Lift and pull out the ash pan, empty it into a metal container, and put the pan back so it sits properly.
Never burn with the ash dump door open. It creates a hazardous condition.

Getting rid of ashes

Use a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Set it on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn, until the cinders have thoroughly cooled. Don't put other waste in it.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
If the glass darkens from slow burning or poor wood, clean it with fireplace glass cleaner once the stove is cold.

  • Never scrape it with anything that might scratch.
  • Don't clean it while it's hot, and don't use abrasive cleaners.
  • Don't slam the door. Check that no logs stick out to hit the glass when you close it.

What the deposit tells you

A light brown, dusty film that wipes off easily usually means good burning and dry wood, so your pipes and chimney are fairly clean. A black, greasy deposit that's hard to remove comes from wet or green wood and burning too slowly. It's building up at least as fast in the chimney.

Cracked or broken glass must be replaced before you use the stove again. Use only ceramic glass, 18" (457mm) x 10-1/4" (260mm) x 5 mm, which your dealer can supply. Don't substitute any other type.

chimney.title: Creosote & chimney fires
chimney.html:
Slow fires make tar and vapours that condense in the cool chimney as creosote. If it catches, creosote burns extremely hot. Some creosote is unavoidable; regular inspection and cleaning is the answer.

  • Have the chimney connector and chimney inspected at least once every two months during the heating season. Remove creosote once it reaches 3 mm. or more.
  • Burn dry, seasoned wood with plenty of air, especially for the first 10 to 30 minutes after loading.
  • Don't turn the stove down too quickly after loading, and don't burn trash, cardboard or Christmas tree limbs.

Signs of a chimney fire

Flames and sparks shooting out of the top of the chimney, a roaring sound, or the chimney vibrating.

If you have a chimney fire

  1. Get ready to evacuate. Everyone should know the plan and the meeting place outside.
  2. Close the air inlet on the stove.
  3. Call the fire department. Keep a fire extinguisher handy.
  4. Afterwards, have the chimney cleaned and checked for stress and cracks before you light another fire. Check the combustibles around the chimney and the roof too.
A certified chimney sweep or installer (NFI, CSIA, WETT or APC) is strongly recommended to inspect and service your chimney.

overfire.title: Over-firing, draft & everyday safety
overfire.html:
Trying to get more heat than the stove is designed for can permanently damage the stove and chimney.

Signs of over-firing: a glowing red top or vent pipe. If the chimney or connector glows, you're over-firing. Not correcting it can be hazardous and may void the warranty.

Draft

Draft is what pulls air through the stove and up the chimney. It depends on the chimney's length, local geography, nearby obstructions and other things.

  • Too much draft can overheat the stove. A fire you can't control, or a glowing red stove part or chimney, is the sign.
  • Too little draft can puff smoke back into the room and plug the chimney. Smoke leaking from the stove or connector joints is the sign.

Everyday safety

  • The stove is hot while it's running. Keep children, clothing and furniture away, and never let children touch the glass.
  • Keep the loading door closed except to add wood, and keep the ash dump closed while burning.
  • Keep wood, furniture and newspapers out of the stove's clearances.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are strongly recommended in the area where the stove is installed.

blower.title: Using the optional blower
blower.html:
The optional blower kit (Part #: 11140001) can be added at any time. It plugs in with a three-prong cord. Keep the cord away from the stove and never under it.

Match it to the air control

  • Air control on "L" (low): run the blower on Low. Otherwise the fire may go out.
  • Air control between "L" and "H": use any blower speed you like.

Auto or manual

Auto: set the rocker switch on the side of the fan housing to "Auto" and pick a speed. The fan comes on as the stove reaches operating temperature, and shuts off after the fire is out and the stove has cooled.

Man: set the rocker switch to "Man" and pick a speed. This skips the temperature sensor, so the blower stays on until you turn it off. You can switch modes or change speed any time.

Vacuum the grill openings on the back and bottom of the blower casing at least every six months to clear dust and debris.

care.title: Gaskets, bricks & regular checks
care.html:
Look these parts over for cracks, heavy corrosion, burned-out sections and bad warping. Call your dealer if you find damage.

WeeklyFirebrick (cracks) · door gasket (sagging, placement, damage)
MonthlyBrick rails and tabs · air riser tube · back of the airwash chamber · baffle locking pin · boost tube cover holes
When the chimney is cleanedTop baffle board / blanket · baffle and baffle gasket · top heat shield and bolts · brick rails · air riser tube
  • Door gasket: it only needs light pressure to seal, which helps it last. Replace it when needed with the kit from your Pacific Energy dealer.
  • Baffle: some warping is normal, up to 1/4" or .65cm. Replace it if it's warped more than that, cracked or broken.
  • Firebrick: replace broken or missing bricks.
  • Keep the front of the firebox, where boost air enters, clear of ash.
Running the stove with broken parts can damage other parts and may void your warranty. Never run it with the baffle or its insulation removed, and use only materials supplied by the manufacturer.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Pacific Energy covers the original registered purchaser:

Limited lifetime (10 years) · parts onlyPorcelain finish, glass (thermal breakage only, not impact), plating, firebox, baffle
3 year comprehensive · parts and laborAny defective part, including blowers, speed controls and thermal switches

Not covered

  • Labor under the lifetime coverage.
  • Firebox rails and heat shields aren't part of the lifetime coverage. Firebrick, gaskets and ceramic fiber blankets aren't warranted.
  • Parts that show misuse, abuse, improper installation, accident, lack of maintenance or modification.

A stove wearing out early usually points to improper use, such as excessive draft, heating too large an area, or contaminated fuel (high sodium, plastics, chemicals). These can void the warranty.

Making a claim

Contact your Pacific Energy dealer with proof of purchase, the purchase date, the model name and the serial number. You can register online at pacificenergy.net/register. The serial number is on the certification label or the manual's cover.

specCombAir.title: Combustion air
specCombAir.html:
Outside air is necessary for mobile homes and optional for residential installs. Consult local code or CAN/CSA-B365 before proceeding.

  • Through the floor: hole large enough for 4" metal flex behind the stove, drawing from a ventilated crawl space or ducted outdoors. Attach the 4" Intake Starter to the Ash Box Enclosure; connect with 4"(100mm) i.d. metal flex pipe.
  • Through the wall behind: 4"(100mm) Air intake; fit the 4" Intake Starter over the hole in the rear of the Ash Box enclosure and run metal flex to the Air Intake.
  • Room air: drawn through the opening in the Ash Box Enclosure into the firebox intake.

Residential outside air requires the stove to be secured to the structure so the duct can't dislodge. Outdoor inlet: 4" (102mm) diameter with rodent screen, hooded vent or 90° elbow turned down; a well-ventilated crawl space doesn't need extending outside.

Negative pressure in the living space can pull gases or fumes indoors. In extreme cold at very slow burn rates the exposed chimney top can ice up and partially block the flue.

59,861 Btu/hr (EPA BTU output range high end)

review.notes: The p. 3 Efficiency and BTU Output table is scrambled in the text extraction; label/value pairs (HHV 72%, LHV 78%, ideal 17 inches, max 18 inches, EPA output 15,845 to 59,861) were confirmed from column positions in the layout file, and HHV < LHV matches the manual's own footnote definitions. The table prints the top of the range as '59.861 btu/hr' (typo); the footnote text gives 59,861 Btu/hr, which the guide uses. Catalog btu_output_epa looks like a rounding of that figure. Rating label also certifies NEOSTONE 2.5 LE; guide uses NEO 2.5 LE only. Not stated in the manual, so not checked or used: heating area, cordwood max output, firebox volume, weight, viewing area, catalytic/non-catalytic. Drawings with unlabeled numbers were not transcribed: Fig. 1 dimensions (p. 12), Fig. 6 residential clearances (p. 15; its values match the label's connector clearances plus 3 in., i.e. to flue center), Fig. 7/8 venting diagrams (p. 18-19; Fig. 7 prints '3" [914 mm]' for the chimney above the roof, text p. 16 says 3 feet (1 m.)), Fig. 13 mobile-home clearances (p. 22), brick placement figures (p. 23-25). Label floor-protector letters G/H/I (USA 16/5/0 in., Canada 18/8/8 in.) have no text definitions, so the guide uses the p. 14 text (USA measured from the fuel loading door opening); label metric for front/firing side (405 mm, 450 mm) differs slightly from p. 14 (406 mm, 457 mm). Label clearance columns (single-wall residential vs double-wall residential and mobile home) were assigned from layout column positions. French-only on the label (p. 3): alcove installs listed with mobile homes as needing the outside air kit ('MAISON MOBILE OU EN ALCOVE'); English names mobile homes only. Not translated. Alcove width metric: English 45"/1.2M, French 45 PO /1.1M. Pages 30-31 are blank. No code table (codes empty); faults come from the p. 26 troubleshooting chart. Warranty prints 'LTD Lifetime Coverage (10 years)' as-is. Catalog marks the model 'not for sale in the USA' (manufacturer site) although this manual carries US clearances and floor protection.
